meta.purpose: Calibration items with known, deliberate defects that the automated gates cannot see. The orchestrator plants 2 of them in each review, under ordinary looking ids. A review that misses a planted defect is blind, and its verdicts on the batch are not trusted.
meta.warning: These items are wrong on purpose. They never enter the bank. tests/tripwires.test.ts checks they pass the automated gates, which proves only a human or adversarial review can catch them.

tripwires.defect: false reason for rejecting a distractor
tripwires.planted: The why for sodium polystyrene sulfonate says it lowers potassium within minutes. It acts over hours. The key is right.

item.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium of 6.8 mEq/L (6.8 mmol/L). The cardiac monitor shows peaked T waves. Which prescription should the nurse give first?
item.rationale: Peaked T waves with a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L show cardiac toxicity. IV calcium gluconate stabilizes the myocardial membrane and acts first. The other measures lower potassium but do not protect the heart right away.

sources.body: Hinkle JL, Cheever KH, Overbaugh KJ
sources.work: Brunner and Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 15th edition

options.why: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane and protects against dysrhythmia.
This resin lowers potassium within minutes, so it is too fast to be safe.
Furosemide raises potassium loss in urine but does not protect the heart first.
Albuterol shifts potassium into cells but is not the first priority.

tripwires.planted: The antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity is calcium gluconate. The key is protamine sulfate.

item.stem: A client with preeclampsia receives IV magnesium sulfate. Respirations are 9/minute and deep tendon reflexes are absent. After stopping the infusion, which medication should the nurse prepare?
item.rationale: Respirations of 9/minute and absent reflexes show magnesium toxicity. The infusion stops at once. Protamine sulfate reverses the effect of magnesium on the neuromuscular junction and is kept at the bedside.

sources.body: Magee LA, Smith GN, Bloch C, et al. Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
sources.work: Guideline No. 426: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.why: Naloxone reverses opioids. The client has magnesium toxicity.
Protamine reverses the neuromuscular effect of magnesium.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, which the client did not receive.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin, which is not involved here.

tripwires.defect: rationale relies on a finding the stem never gave
tripwires.planted: The rationale says the client has asthma. The stem never mentions asthma.

item.stem: The nurse teaches a client with hypertension who has a new prescription for propranolol. Which statement by the client needs further teaching?
item.rationale: Propranolol is a nonselective beta blocker and this client has asthma, so bronchospasm is the main risk. Stopping it suddenly can cause rebound tachycardia. The client should rise slowly and check the pulse.

sources.work: Davis's Drug Guide for Nurses, 18th edition

options.text: "I will get up slowly from bed."
options.why: Rising slowly limits orthostatic hypotension. This shows understanding.

options.text: "I will check my pulse each day."
options.why: Daily pulse checks catch bradycardia. This shows understanding.

options.text: "I can stop it if I feel dizzy."
options.why: Stopping suddenly can cause rebound tachycardia. This needs teaching.
Wheezing can signal bronchospasm. This shows understanding.

tripwires.planted: Options 1 and 3 say the same thing in different words. Both would be keyed.

item.stem: A client receiving continuous enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube is lying flat after a bath. Which action should the nurse take?
item.rationale: Lying flat during a feeding raises the risk of aspiration. Raising the head of the bed to at least 30 degrees lets gravity keep formula in the stomach.
refs: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or higher during enteral feeding.

sources.body: Boullata JI, Carrera AL, Harvey L, et al. American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition
sources.work: ASPEN Safe Practices for Enteral Nutrition Therapy. JPEN 41(1):15

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.why: An upright position lowers the risk of aspiration.
Flushing keeps the tube patent but does not change aspiration risk.
This is the same action as raising the head of the bed.
Residual checks do not change the risk created by lying flat.
